document.abstract: The limited contrast and colors in standard dynamic range (SDR) have historically compelled content producers to make hard choices, whereas high dynamic range (HDR) offers them the possibility to show more—meaning telling stories with greater freedom and flexibility. Even so, HDR content presents a challenge of its own. The wide variation in capabilities among HDR displays conflicts with the desire to have any HDR or SDR production play optimally on any display, regardless of whether it is HDR or SDR. Tone mapping is the generic term for the operation that addresses this issue, whether tone compression, which maps from HDR to a lower-luminance HDR or SDR, or tone expansion, which maps from SDR or HDR to a higher-luminance HDR. Though the trend is to produce the highest quality content in HDR, legacy content is ever present, and lots of new content is still produced in SDR. Mixing feeds in production requires tone expansion for SDR content to match the HDR. Distribution paths can then require tone compression back to SDR without degradation. In this context, a perfect SDR–HDR–SDR roundtrip conversion is required to preserve artistic intent for all content. Furthermore, in a live context, such tools need to be automatic and low latency. This article discusses various tone-mapping techniques, including static solutions such as lookup tables (LUTs) and dynamic solutions based on metadata. The relative advantages are considered, and the performance of each is analyzed. Particular attention is paid to the roundtrip performance, which is important to content producers mastering both SDR and HDR sources, yet wanting to exploit the full range of storytelling capabilities an HDR stream can offer. Test results using a proposed solution that has been introduced in practice, “Advanced HDR by TechnicolorⓇ,” are described.

authors.bio: David Touze works as a system architect at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He has a background in hardware design, system architecture, and image/video processing. He and his team are researching new video formats with a major focus on HDR and WCG techniques adapted to live video production and distribution workflows.
authors.name: David Touze

authors.bio: Frederic Plissonneaugraduated from INSA, Rennes, France, in 1988 and has worked in the video compression domain as an engineer/team leader and project leader in the field of ASIC technologies. He is currently focused on HDR within R&I Video Lab, Rennes.
authors.name: Frederic Plissonneau

authors.bio: Bill Redmann is the director of Standards for Immersive Media Technologies at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He contributes to Next-Gen Media standards in several standards organizations. A SMPTE Fellow, he holds 84 U.S. patents, plus an MS degree in engineering from the University of California, Los Angeles, CA.
authors.name: Bill Redmann

authors.bio: Robin Le Naour is a senior engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He has a background in real time software development, system architecture and image/video processing. He currently works on HDR at the R&I Video Lab, Rennes, France.
authors.name: Robin Le Naour

authors.bio: Patrick Lopez is a researcher at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He is skilled in signal processing and developed algorithms for digital modulation and then video compression. He is currently involved in the HDR development team, focused on algorithmic development in tone mapping.
authors.name: Patrick Lopez

authors.bio: Patrick Morvan is a senior research and development engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He joined Thomson Research Labs, Rennes, France, in 1990. He has been involved in several innovative projects aimed at developing new video formats. Over the past 15 years, he has developed an expertise in color science for cinema and broadcast applications. His current research is focused on color management and perception for high dynamic range workflows.
authors.name: Patrick Morvan

authors.bio: Laurent Cauvin is a senior engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He has been working on image and video processing since 1985. He is now involved in HDR imaging, mainly in the inverse tone mapping domain (algorithms, system architecture, and hardware and software porting).
authors.name: Laurent Cauvin

authors.bio: Nick Mitchell is an accomplished entertainment technology professional with two decades of experience. As CTO and senior technology consultant at WildAcre Company, his technology and creative services firm, he plays a pivotal role in developing and delivering innovative technologies, strategies, and services for a diverse range of organizations.
authors.name: Nick Mitchell

authors.bio: Alan Stein leads InterDigital’s Visual Standards team of technical experts participating in video standards and industry forums. He is a board member and marketing chair of MC-IF and long-time chair of ATSC’s TG3/S41 group, the video group for ATSC 3.0. He received ATSC’s Bernard Lechner Award in 2021. He holds 17 patents in the realm of digital video.
authors.name: Alan Stein
